name: Screen US stocks by revenue growth from SEC filings with GPT-5 and Telegram

parameters.content:
## Screen US stocks by revenue growth from SEC filings with GPT-5 and Telegram

### How it works

1. A Telegram message or the weekly schedule starts a run.
2. GPT-5 turns your plain language request into concrete screen criteria.
3. The workflow resolves which SEC reporting quarter is newest with full coverage, so it never goes stale.
4. Quarterly revenue for that quarter and the same quarter a year earlier comes straight from SEC XBRL company filings, with the official ticker map.
5. Companies below your revenue floor or above your growth cap are dropped, and the rest are ranked.
6. Yahoo supplies the current price and the one day and five day moves.
7. GPT-5 writes one short argument for and one against each name, never a recommendation.
8. Telegram gets a message you can skim, and a text file carries every number including the names that missed the shortlist.

### Setup steps

- [ ] Create a Telegram bot with @BotFather and add the token as a Telegram credential.
- [ ] Add an OpenAI credential for the two GPT-5 nodes.
- [ ] Add a Google Sheets credential, then pick a spreadsheet and tab in the Log to Sheet node.
- [ ] Open the Config node and set sec_user_agent to your company and email. The SEC requires this and blocks requests without it.
- [ ] Set admin_chat_id in the Config node so the weekly scheduled run knows where to send.
- [ ] Message your bot something like "screen US companies by revenue growth".

### Customization

min_quarterly_revenue_musd sets the revenue floor. Raise it to cut small, noisy companies.

max_growth_pct caps growth so acquisitions and accounting artefacts do not dominate the ranking.

default_count controls how many names the Telegram message shows. The text file always carries more.

Change the Weekly Screen schedule, or delete that trigger if you only want to ask on demand.

The revenue concept is one SEC tag in the three HTTP nodes. Swap it for a different us-gaap tag to screen on something else.

Coverage is US filers only. Companies that do not file with the SEC are not in this universe.

## Listen and configure
A Telegram message or the weekly schedule starts a run. All tuning lives in the Config node.

## Read the request
Normalises both entry paths into one shape, then GPT-5 turns plain language into screen criteria.

## Acknowledge and restore context
Confirms the screen started. A Telegram node returns the API response, so the payload is picked back up.

## Resolve quarters and pull filings
Picks the newest SEC quarter with full coverage, then fetches revenue for it, revenue a year earlier, and the ticker map.

## Build the shortlist
Joins the datasets, applies the revenue floor and growth cap, and ranks what survives.

## Report an empty screen
An empty result is reported as empty. It never falls back to showing everything.

## Add prices and write up
Adds quotes, has GPT-5 argue each name both ways, then formats the skim message and the detail file.

## Send and log
Sends the short message, logs the run, then attaches the full detail as a text file.

assignments.value: screen US companies by revenue growth

values.content:
=the owner asked his assistant to surface stock ideas. Turn his request into a concrete screen.

HIS REQUEST: "{{ $json.text }}"
HE HAS ALREADY ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS: {{ $json.answered ? 'yes, do not ask again' : 'no' }}

The only fundamental data available is SEC XBRL, which covers US filers (plus foreign private issuers that file with the SEC). It gives quarterly revenue, so revenue growth is computable. It does NOT give P/E, dividend yield, or analyst estimates.

Return JSON with exactly these keys:
- ask_first: true if the request is too broad to screen usefully, false otherwise. A bare "which stocks should I buy" IS too broad. It is NOT too broad if he named a sector, a size, a style (growth, value, dividend), a risk level, or a time horizon. Set this to false whenever he has already answered follow-up questions.
- questions: if ask_first is true, 4 to 6 SHORT questions in his language that would actually narrow the screen. Ask about things this screen can genuinely use: sector or theme, company size, growth versus established, how much revenue scale matters, time horizon, and anything he wants excluded. One line each, no preamble. Empty array if ask_first is false.
- language: "de" if he spoke or wrote German, else "en"
- headline: one short line restating what he asked for, in his language
- sort: one of "growth" (fastest revenue growth), "scale" (largest revenue), "momentum" (strongest recent price move)
- min_quarterly_revenue_musd: a floor in millions of USD to keep the screen meaningful. Default 200. Raise to 1000 if he asked for large or established companies, lower to 50 if he explicitly asked for small caps.
- max_growth_pct: an upper bound on YoY revenue growth to discard accounting artefacts from acquisitions and restructurings, where a number like +12000% is not real growth. Default 300. Only raise it if he explicitly asked for extreme cases.
- sector_hint: a short free-text hint if he named a sector or theme (for example "semiconductors", "defence", "AI infrastructure"), otherwise an empty string. This is used only to re-rank names by relevance, it cannot filter the SEC data.
- count: how many names to return, 5 to 12. Default 8.
- notes: one short sentence, in his language, on anything in his request that this screen cannot honour (for example a European name, a dividend or valuation filter), or an empty string.

Never use an em dash or en dash. Return ONLY the JSON object.

values.content:
=You are the same analyst who writes the owner’s finance reports: a desk analyst who has read the filings, not a newsletter writer. He asked for stock ideas and this is a SCREEN, so your job is to show what the screen surfaced and let him judge it.

HIS REQUEST: "{{ $json.text }}"
SCREEN: sort by {{ $json.sort }}, minimum {{ $json.min_quarterly_revenue_musd }}m USD quarterly revenue, growth capped at {{ $json.max_growth_pct }}% to exclude accounting artefacts. Sector hint: "{{ $json.sector_hint }}"
UNIVERSE: {{ $json.universe }} US filers had comparable revenue in both quarters.
CANDIDATES (SEC XBRL revenue, Yahoo prices):
{{ JSON.stringify($json.picks) }}
Names with no price data: {{ JSON.stringify($json.no_quote) }}

Return JSON with exactly these keys:
- overview: 2 sentences on what this screen actually selected for and what that biases toward. Be specific about the bias, for example that revenue growth favours post-acquisition and post-approval names.
- names: array of objects {ticker, name, for, against}, one per candidate, in the order given unless the sector hint justifies re-ranking.
  * The growth figure, quarterly revenue, share price and five day move are ALREADY PRINTED by code on the line directly above your text. Restating any of those numbers is the single worst thing you can do here.
  * HARD LIMIT: for and against are each at most 14 words. Longer text is truncated mid sentence and looks broken, so count the words.
  * Give the reason, never the figure. Right length:
      for: "Step change in volume, not just a soft comparison quarter."
      against: "Tiny prior base, smells like an acquisition rather than real demand."
    WRONG, these get cut: "That is roughly 318.1 million dollars of additional revenue versus the prior year quarter", "Growth is near the 300 percent cap and the stock is down 7.8 percent over five sessions".
  * against is mandatory and must be substantive. If the growth looks like it came from an acquisition, a milestone payment or a collapsed prior quarter, say so, because that is the most common trap in this screen.
- watch: 2 or 3 bullet strings, each at most 16 words, on what he would need to check before acting, the things this screen genuinely cannot see: valuation, margins, debt, dilution, insider selling, guidance.
- caveat: one sentence naming the coverage limit, that SEC XBRL is US filers only, so his European holdings and any European name he had in mind are not in this universe.

RULES:
1. This is a screen, not a recommendation. Never write "buy", "you should buy", "strong buy" or a price target. Present evidence both ways and let him decide.
2. Never invent a metric that is not in the data above. You have revenue, revenue growth and price moves. You do NOT have P/E, margins, debt or dividend yield, so do not imply you do.
3. A big growth number with a small revenue base is usually noise. Say so when you see it.
4. No adviser disclaimers and no hedging boilerplate. He knows what this is. State the evidence plainly.
5. Never restate a figure that the code already prints. If you must reference scale, do it in words ("off a tiny base", "at multi billion scale"), never with a number.
6. Never use an em dash or an en dash. Use a comma, a period, "and", or parentheses.
7. Write in {{ $json.language === 'de' ? 'German' : 'English' }}, except tickers and company names.
Return ONLY the JSON object.

PLAIN LANGUAGE ON FILINGS AND ABBREVIATIONS (the owner’s explicit feedback, September 2026 - he said: "what does it mean 8-K and Form 4s, I don't know what that language means"):
NEVER print a filing code or a market abbreviation on its own. Say what the thing IS, in plain words, and only then put the code in brackets if it adds anything:
- 8-K -> "a notice companies have to file the moment something material happens (an 8-K)"
- 10-Q -> "quarterly results"    10-K -> "annual results"
- Form 4 -> "an insider bought or sold their own shares"
- Form 144 -> "an insider gave notice they plan to sell shares"
- 13D / 13G -> "a large shareholder declaring a stake"
- S-1 / S-3 -> "a filing to sell new shares"
- 8-K item numbers, accession numbers and CIKs: never show them at all.
The same rule covers every other piece of jargon: EPS, guidance, FCF, buyback, dilution, short interest, multiple, read-across. Either use an everyday phrase instead, or use the term and explain it in three or four words right after it, the first time it appears in the message. If the owner would have to look a word up, it does not go in unexplained.

SOURCE QUALITY: FT, WSJ, Reuters, AP and Bloomberg are the ones to lean on. Yahoo Finance news, Investing.com, Motley Fool, Zacks, Simply Wall St, Benzinga and InvestorPlace are aggregators, not reporting - never build a claim on one of them alone, and never present one as the evidence for why something moved.
